summary: Specifies methods for characterizing how a device behaves while it performs an In-Service Software Upgrade (ISSU), where the aim is to limit disruption to the control and data planes during planned software changes.

plainLanguage.summary: This measures how well a machine keeps working while you upgrade it, like changing a tire on a moving toy car.

questions: how to benchmark in-service software upgrade
how to measure packet loss during upgrade
subtitle: Testing how network devices behave when upgraded without stopping the network

tldr.problem: Network devices need to upgrade their software, but doing so typically stops service. This RFC defines how to measure whether a device can upgrade with minimal disruption.
tldr.mechanism: It specifies test procedures that measure control-plane and data-plane outages during an In-Service Software Upgrade (ISSU), using a load model to simulate production network traffic.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can now benchmark and compare how well devices maintain service during upgrades, helping them plan maintenance with greater confidence.

facts.label: Traffic measurement
facts.value: Frames per second and bits per second

today: RFC 7654 is an Informational RFC providing benchmarking guidance that is actively used by network operators and vendors to evaluate and compare ISSU implementations.

sections.title: The Need to Upgrade Without Stopping
sections.content:
In-Service Software Upgrade (ISSU) lets a network device update its software while continuing to forward traffic, minimizing downtime and service disruption. Service providers require this capability because network failures cause costly outages. However, testing ISSU is difficult: how do you measure whether a device truly maintains service, and how much data is lost during the upgrade?

This RFC specifies benchmarking procedures to characterize ISSU behavior quantitatively. The goal is to answer: How long is control-plane service unavailable? How many packets are lost during the upgrade? How long does the device take to recover? Operators need answers to plan maintenance windows and evaluate which devices are reliable.
sections.plainLanguage: When you upgrade software on a running network device, you want to know: does everything still work? This RFC explains how to measure and report that fairly.

sections.title: The Phases of an ISSU
sections.content:
ISSU proceeds in four phases. Software Download transfers the new version to the device, typically performed before the maintenance window to avoid timing skew. Software Staging loads the software onto redundant components (like a secondary routing processor) and checks compatibility. Upgrade Run is the critical phase: the secondary processor takes over and becomes primary, while the primary upgrades. This phase is where control-plane and data-plane outages occur. Upgrade Acceptance completes the upgrade once both processors run the new code and redundancy is restored.

The RFC emphasizes that implementations vary: some vendors may combine stages, and some features (like Bidirectional Failure Detection) may not support ISSU at all. The test operator must understand the device's capabilities and the production environment the device will face.
sections.plainLanguage: ISSU has four steps: get the new software, prepare to switch over, actually switch, and confirm everything works. Each step has different risks.

sections.title: How to Test: Topology and Load
sections.content:
Testing requires an isolated test environment that closely mimics production. The test topology should include the same hardware configuration, line cards, memory, and initial software as the production device. For the network load, the RFC recommends mimicking existing production data- and control-plane information, including Layer 1 through Layer 3 communications, multicast traffic, and VPNs if deployed. Traffic MUST be distributed across multiple source-destination pairs with varying prefix lengths.

The load model must apply sufficient traffic to permit timing measurements at 100-millisecond granularity (e.g., 100 Mbps on a 10 Gbps interface). Steady traffic streams are preferred over bursty loads to simplify analysis. The RFC strongly recommends deploying a Network Management System (NMS) to monitor the device during testing and to detect interference with management traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: You build a test network that looks like a real one, then send realistic traffic through it. You measure what happens when you upgrade during that traffic.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Test Procedures
sections.content:
Before the ISSU, verify that the device has enough disk space, that redundancy is synchronized, and that routing is stable. Document a baseline of CPU, memory, traffic volumes, and routing information. During Software Staging, establish all protocol adjacencies, clear relevant logs and interface counters, apply the load, document the baseline, then note the start time (T0) and begin the code change. Monitor the secondary RP's reload and note completion time as T1.

During Upgrade Run, note the start time and initiate the upgrade. Monitor closely for control-plane disruptions and traffic loss. Once the DUT converges on the new code and returns to normal operation, note the completion time and log the duration as T2. Record the number of frames lost (TPL_frames) and calculate the outage duration (TPL_time in milliseconds). After the upgrade, verify the DUT status, check that memory and CPU have returned to baseline, and perform configuration and routing table verification.
sections.plainLanguage: The test has three main measurements: how long does the secondary RP take to reload (T1), how long does the actual upgrade take (T2), and how many packets get lost (TPL_time).

sections.title: Results and Data Reporting
sections.content:
Results MUST report at least the following: DUT hardware and software details, test topology diagram, load model description, measured times (T1, T2, T3 for redundancy restoration, T4 for total maintenance window), traffic disruption data, and any anomalies observed. The RFC provides a table of recommended parameters to report, including traffic load (frames per second and bits per second), frame loss, impact time in milliseconds, protocols tested (IPv4, IPv6, MPLS), frame size, port media, port speed, interface encapsulation types, and number of prefixes.

Importantly, the RFC warns that the DUT's own counters and data collection may be inaccurate during ISSU. Instead, rely on external test tools and equipment to measure packet loss and timing. For optional stress testing under route churn, the RFC defines how to introduce controlled route flaps during the ISSU phases.
sections.plainLanguage: Report all the timing numbers, packet loss, what hardware you tested, and what production scenario it matched. Use numbers from the test tools, not from the device itself.
